# AN/PRC-117G Radio
The AN/PRC-117G is a manpack radio used to carry, relay, and monitor field radio nets. It stores up to four net memories and can be used either worn by an operator or deployed as a retransmission station.
Exact ranges and modifiers are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Basic Operation
A powered radio can be programmed while held, worn, or lying on the ground. The set only needs to be worn or deployed when it must transmit, relay traffic, run a radio check, search the band, or print its log.
To place a set in service:
- Open [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold] from the radio's verb menu. - Switch the set on with [bold]6 PWR[/bold], or move the function switch to [bold]CT[/bold] or [bold]PT[/bold]. - Open [bold]PGM[/bold], move the cursor to [bold]ADD NET[/bold], and press [bold]ENT[/bold]. - Key a short label on the letter keys and press [bold]ENT[/bold]. - Move the cursor to the new memory and press [bold]ENT[/bold] to open it. - Choose [bold]TUNE TO A NET[/bold] or [bold]KEY A FREQUENCY[/bold]. - Return to the memory and choose [bold]WORK THIS NET[/bold] to make it active. - Insert the matching COMSEC fill card when the net requires one. - Wear the set in the [bold]back slot[/bold], or deploy it with [bold]Set Up Retrans[/bold].
Transmit through the active memory with:
[color=#a4885c]:r Message here.[/color]
A worn radio normally uses the wearer's assigned callsign. If none is assigned, it transmits as [bold]UNKNOWN STATION[/bold].
## Operator Access
Only trained radio operators can open the AN/PRC panel or transmit directly through the set.
[bold]GOVFOR and OPFOR[/bold] trained roles include Commander, Adjutant, staff officers, engineering officers, intelligence officers, synthetics, squad leaders, Fireteam Leaders, and Radio Traffic Operators.
[bold]CLF[/bold] trained roles are the Cell Leader and Radio Operator.
Reading a [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold] permanently grants radio training regardless of role.
Nearby headset users do not need radio training to use a relay. The radio only needs to be powered, deployed, carrying the correct net, and operated by a trained wearer when worn.
## Panel Status
The display reports the current memory, COMSEC state, signal, battery, and built-in test status.
- [bold]RX[/bold] and [bold]TX[/bold] show receive and transmit activity. - [bold]SEC[/bold], [bold]UNSEC[/bold], or [bold]CLEAR[/bold] shows the security state of outgoing traffic. - [bold]SIG[/bold] shows relay signal strength. Direct-frequency memories display [bold]--DIR--[/bold]. - [bold]BAT[/bold] shows battery state. - [bold]BIT[/bold] reports whether the set is ready.
[bold]BIT[/bold] [bold]Meaning[/bold]
[bold]PASS[/bold] Powered, deployed, and on a working memory.
[bold]NO CELL[/bold] No battery is fitted. The set cannot switch on.
[bold]OFF[/bold] The set is switched off.
[bold]STOWED[/bold] The set is powered and programmable, but is neither worn nor deployed.
[bold]SRCH[/bold] The search receiver is active. Normal receive and transmit are suspended.
[bold]NO NET[/bold] No working memory is selected.
## Function Switch
[bold]Position[/bold] [bold]Function[/bold]
[bold]OFF[/bold] Switches the set off.
[bold]CT[/bold] Secure operation. Moving the switch to CT again steps through FH, SC, and CT.
[bold]PT[/bold] Plain-text operation.
[bold]LD[/bold] Opens the COMSEC page, then springs back to the previous fixed position.
[bold]Z[/bold] Opens the COMSEC page with zeroize armed, then springs back to the previous fixed position.
[bold]LD[/bold] and [bold]Z[/bold] are momentary detents. Their actions remain in effect after the switch returns; returning to CT or PT does not cancel an armed COMSEC action or change the selected waveform.
## Keypad and Pages
### Working the screen
Every control is on the display. There are no buttons below it.
- [bold]PRE[/bold] moves the cursor up and down the lines. - [bold]ENT[/bold] works the line under the cursor: it steps a setting, opens a list, or runs an action. - [bold]CLR[/bold] backs out one screen. - The soft keys below the glass page between screens. - A line can also be clicked. The first click moves the cursor to it; the second works it.
A line marked [bold]>[/bold] is the one the cursor is on. Lines that cannot be worked are dimmed.
### Keypad
Number keys fill in whatever field the screen has opened. Otherwise they perform the function printed above the key.
- [bold]1 CALL[/bold] runs a radio check. - [bold]2 LT[/bold] controls the backlight. - [bold]3 MODE[/bold] changes waveform. - [bold]4 SQL[/bold] changes squelch. - [bold]5 ZERO[/bold] opens COMSEC with zeroize armed. - [bold]6 PWR[/bold] switches the set on or off. - [bold]7 OPT[/bold], [bold]8 PGM[/bold], [bold]9 SEC[/bold], and [bold]0 LOG[/bold] open their pages. - [bold]VOL[/bold] changes speaker volume. - [bold]PRE[/bold] moves the cursor. - [bold]CLR[/bold] backs out, or removes the last keyed character. - [bold]ENT[/bold] works the line under the cursor, or confirms a keyed value.
Text fields use the letters printed above each number key. Press a key once for the first letter of its group and again to step through the group; pausing, or moving to another key, settles the character. [bold]CLR[/bold] rubs out and [bold]ENT[/bold] confirms.
The [bold]?[/bold] page contains the same control summary.
The main pages are:
- [bold]PGM[/bold] — memories, labels, tuning, and active-memory selection. - [bold]SEC[/bold] — COMSEC fill, zeroize, destroy, and recrypto. - [bold]SRCH[/bold] — band search and discovered contacts. - [bold]LOG[/bold] — received and transmitted traffic, filters, and printing. - [bold]OPT[/bold] — waveform, monitor, scan, squelch, transmit power, speaker, callsign, and status. - [bold]?[/bold] — keypad reference.
## Net Memories
The radio stores up to [bold]four[/bold] memories. A memory may contain a named faction net or a direct frequency.
The memory marked [bold]*[/bold] is the active one. [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] always uses it.
Press [bold]ENT[/bold] on a memory to open it. That screen carries everything that can be done to it:
- [bold]WORK THIS NET[/bold] makes the memory active. - [bold]TUNE TO A NET[/bold] lists the nets this set is entitled to. - [bold]KEY A FREQUENCY[/bold] takes a direct frequency off the keypad. - [bold]EMPTY THE MEMORY[/bold] removes the tuned net or frequency but keeps the memory and its label. - [bold]DELETE THE MEMORY[/bold] removes the memory entirely. - [bold]RENAME[/bold] relabels it. The memory is rebuilt, so its contents are cleared.
Frequencies are entered against the [bold]___.___[/bold] template. Unentered positions are treated as zero. [bold]CLR[/bold] removes the last digit and [bold]ENT[/bold] confirms the value.
If the entered frequency belongs to a known net, the radio loads that net. Otherwise it is stored as a direct frequency if it falls within a supported band.
## Callsigns
Radio traffic is identified by callsign rather than character name or job title. Face-to-face speech is unaffected.
A worn AN/PRC follows the wearer's assigned callsign by default. The callsign field displays [bold]AUTO[/bold] in this state and updates when the wearer or assignment changes.
A fixed station callsign can be set from [bold]OPT[/bold]. Choose a preset or enter a callsign of up to 16 characters, then select [bold]SET[/bold]. Clear the field and select [bold]SET[/bold] again to return to automatic assignment.
The [bold]Comms Net Directory[/bold] shows current callsign assignments. It is available from command-post systems and, where issued, from [bold]NET DIRECTORY[/bold] on the radio's OPT page. Enemy directories cannot be opened by an unauthorized faction.
Common callsign forms include:
[bold]Example[/bold] [bold]Station[/bold]
HAVOC 6 Commanding officer
HAVOC 5 Executive officer or second-in-command
HAVOC 7 Senior non-commissioned officer
HAVOC ROMEO Command radio operator
SABRE ACTUAL Sabre squad leader
SABRE ROMEO Radio operator attached to Sabre
[bold]ACTUAL[/bold] identifies the person in command speaking personally rather than an operator speaking on the station's behalf.
For transmission format and prowords, see [textlink="Voice Procedure" link="AU14CommsVoiceProcedure"].
## Handset
The handset lets a nearby person use the radio's active memory without radio training.
Alt-click the wearer or a deployed radio and select [bold]Take Handset[/bold]. Only one person can hold it at a time, and the user must remain within cord range.
The handset uses the handset user's callsign. Returning it or moving out of range disconnects it.
## Direct Frequencies
A direct-frequency memory is not tied to a named net. A [textlink="tuned headset" link="AU14CommsHeadsets"] on the same frequency can use [color=#a4885c]:x[/color], while the AN/PRC uses [color=#a4885c]:r[/color].
Direct-frequency traffic is short-ranged unless a powered, deployed AN/PRC carries the same frequency and bridges nearby users. Exact ranges are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Operating Modes
[bold]MODE[/bold] on OPT, [bold]3 MODE[/bold], and the function switch all change the same setting.
[bold]Mode[/bold] [bold]Use[/bold] [bold]Advantages[/bold] [bold]Limits[/bold]
[bold]FH[/bold] Frequency-hopping traffic. Reduces jamming by one tier. Higher battery use and a small direction-finding signature.
[bold]SC[/bold] Normal secured traffic. Efficient and no direction-finding signature while secured. No jamming resistance.
[bold]CT[/bold] Cipher traffic between compatible AN/PRCs. Unreadable without matching fill and no direction-finding signature while secured. Requires matching fill and is not received by standard headsets.
[bold]PT[/bold] Plain-text broadcast. Lowest battery use. Readable by compatible receivers and produces the strongest direction-finding signature.
## Monitor, Scan, and Squelch
[bold]MON[/bold] enables receive-only monitoring. The set receives loaded nets, but [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] is blocked.
[bold]SCAN[/bold] listens across all loaded memories. When traffic arrives, the receiving memory becomes active and remains active until changed again.
[bold]SQL[/bold] controls how much degraded traffic is allowed through. Lower values pass more static and weak traffic; higher values suppress more damaged traffic. Squelch does not improve a signal.
Exact squelch thresholds are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Speaker
[bold]VOL[/bold] controls the radio's speaker.
- [bold]MUTE[/bold] silences the speaker. Logging and handset use continue. - [bold]LOW[/bold] is audible to the operator only. - [bold]MED[/bold], [bold]HIGH[/bold], and [bold]MAX[/bold] make received traffic audible to nearby people at increasing distance.
A person who already receives the same traffic through their own headset does not hear a duplicate copy from the radio speaker.
## COMSEC Fill
Secure traffic requires a matching physical fill card in the radio.
The SEC page shows [bold]SECURED[/bold] when the loaded fill matches the traffic being used. Faction headsets contain their own keys; the AN/PRC does not.
If a secured faction net is used without matching fill, the radio warns the operator but still transmits the message in the clear.
A current captured fill card can be inserted into a compatible AN/PRC to decode that faction's secured traffic until the faction performs recrypto.
### ZEROIZE
[bold]ZEROIZE[/bold] ejects the loaded fill card without damaging it. The card is placed in a free hand or dropped nearby if no hand is available.
### DESTROY
[bold]DESTROY[/bold] permanently removes the loaded fill card.
### RECRYPTO
[bold]RECRYPTO[/bold] advances the active fill generation for the card's faction. It requires the appropriate command authority.
Older cards from that faction become [bold]STALE[/bold]. A stale card remains identifiable but cannot secure or decode current traffic.
ZEROIZE, DESTROY, and RECRYPTO use a confirmation window. The first activation arms the action; a second activation within four seconds commits it.
## Transmit Power and Antennas
[bold]PWR[/bold] on the OPT page changes transmit power. Higher power increases relay range, battery use, and direction-finding signature where applicable.
The standard [bold]whip antenna[/bold] is intended for mobile use. A [bold]mast antenna[/bold] provides greater stationary range but performs poorly while moving.
Exact multipliers are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Jamming and Direction Finding
FH reduces jamming by one tier. AN/PRC traffic can still be transmitted from inside a jammer field, although the message may be degraded.
Direction-finding equipment can detect transmissions that create a signature. PT traffic, unsecured faction-net traffic, FH traffic, higher transmit power, repeated transmissions, and transmissions near enemy jamming all increase detection risk.
Secured SC and CT traffic do not create a direction-finding signature.
## Radio Check
[bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold] on OPT, or [bold]1 CALL[/bold], tests the active net. The radio transmits:
[bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold]
The operator receives a private report listing stations in clear or degraded coverage. When performed inside enemy jamming, the report also includes a bearing to the strongest jammer.
RADIO CHECK requires the radio to be worn or deployed.
## Retransmission Stations
A trained operator can deploy a radio with [bold]Set Up Retrans[/bold]. A deployed radio:
- Relays its loaded faction nets. - Continues recording traffic. - Uses battery power. - Keeps its memories, labels, and fill card. - Allows nearby users to take its handset.
Any character can select [bold]Pack Up Radio[/bold]. A captured retransmission station therefore remains usable as equipment if the captor can operate it.
## Fixed Infrastructure
Faction combat nets require at least one active coverage source. Depending on the faction and location, this may be:
- A worn AN/PRC. - A deployed retransmission station. - A command-post antenna mast. - A powered communications array. - A vehicle radio. - A field antenna mast. - CLF-specific base stations, relay sets, or feeder taps.
Masts, worn radios, and retransmission stations normally reach one level above or below their own. Shipboard communications arrays provide site-wide vertical coverage while powered.
Colony and civilian channels are not relay-gated.
## CLF Communications
The CLF use two relay-gated combat nets:
- [bold]CLF[/bold] — the cell net carried by CLF earpieces. - [bold]CLF Command[/bold] — an AN/PRC-only command net.
CLF manpacks are issued with both nets already loaded as [bold]CELL[/bold] and [bold]CMD[/bold].
CLF coverage can come from a worn manpack, a clandestine base station, a relay set, a field mast, or a feeder tap installed on compatible fixed infrastructure. The CLF have no native communications array.
The clandestine base station is too heavy to wear and only operates while deployed. It is issued already tuned to both CLF nets and can be used through its handset.
For net-splicing values and infrastructure ranges, see [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## SEARCH
[bold]START SEARCH[/bold] sweeps the searchable radio band for recent transmissions.
While search is active:
- The radio leaves all loaded nets. - Normal receiving stops. - Transmission is inhibited. - Battery drain continues.
Search contacts gain confidence when the receiver catches repeated transmissions on the same frequency. Low-confidence contacts remain hidden, partial contacts show an approximate frequency, and full-confidence contacts reveal the exact frequency and net name. A fully resolved contact can be loaded into the active memory by pressing [bold]ENT[/bold] on it.
Partial contacts decay if the frequency is not heard again. A fully resolved contact remains known for the operation.
Search only detects frequencies inside its receiver band. Direct frequencies outside that band are not discoverable through SEARCH.
Exact search timing, range, and confidence values are listed in [textlink="Comms Quick Reference" link="AU14CommsQuickRef"].
## Intercepting Traffic
Another faction's frequency can be entered manually or loaded from a resolved SEARCH contact.
Intercepted traffic appears in [color=#FF6B6B]red[/color] and is marked [bold]INTERCEPT[/bold] in the log.
Reception depends on the transmitting station's mode and COMSEC state:
[bold]Traffic[/bold] [bold]Without matching fill[/bold]
Headset traffic Static.
Secured AN/PRC traffic Static.
Unsecured AN/PRC traffic Readable.
PT traffic Readable.
FH sent in the clear Readable with light interference.
CT traffic Not displayed.
A matching current fill card allows compatible secured traffic to be decoded until recrypto makes the card stale.
Tuning an enemy frequency does not extend that faction's coverage. AN/PRCs relay only their own faction's named nets.
## Net Log
The radio stores the last [bold]50[/bold] log entries while powered. It records AN/PRC transmissions, the wearer's headset transmissions, incoming traffic on the active memory, and additional loaded-net traffic while MON or SCAN is active.
[bold]PRINT LOG[/bold] prints the full log. [bold]PRINT INTERCEPTS[/bold] prints only entries marked INTERCEPT. Printing requires the radio to be worn or deployed.
## Connector Plate
The connector labels on the left side of the panel report installed equipment:
- [bold]J8/J5 ANT[/bold] — fitted antenna. - [bold]J1 AUDIO[/bold] — handset or speaker output. - [bold]J4 KDU/FILL[/bold] — loaded COMSEC fill; stale fill is shown in red. - [bold]J2 PWR/GPS[/bold] — battery charge.
